steps.title: Performance vs. scalability
steps.body: A system has a performance problem when it is slow for a single user. It has a scalability problem when it is fast for one user but slow under heavy load. A service is scalable if adding resources increases its performance in proportion to the resources added.

steps.prompt: Your app is fast when you test it alone, but slows down badly when 10,000 users arrive. What kind of problem is this?
steps.explanation: Fast for one user but slow under load is the definition of a scalability problem. A performance problem would be slow even for a single user.

steps.title: Latency vs. throughput
steps.body: Latency is the time it takes to perform one action or produce one result. Throughput is how many of those actions are completed per unit of time. A common goal is the highest throughput possible while keeping latency acceptable.

steps.prompt: An API handles 2,000 requests per second, and each request takes 80 ms. Which number is the throughput?
steps.explanation: Throughput counts completed actions per unit of time (2,000 per second). The 80 ms is latency: how long one request takes.

steps.prompt: What is the usual goal when tuning latency and throughput?
steps.explanation: Systems aim to serve as much work as possible (throughput) while each request still finishes fast enough for users (acceptable latency).

steps.title: Vertical vs. horizontal scaling
steps.body: Vertical scaling means giving one machine more power (CPU, memory). It is simple but has a hardware ceiling and expensive top-end machines. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines. Using many commodity servers is usually more cost-efficient and more available, but it adds complexity: servers should be stateless, with user sessions kept in a shared store such as a database or a cache like Redis.

steps.prompt: Which is a real downside of horizontal scaling?

choices.text: It has a hard ceiling set by the biggest machine you can buy
It adds complexity, such as keeping servers stateless

steps.explanation: More machines means more moving parts: servers must be stateless and sessions moved to a shared store. The hardware ceiling is the downside of vertical scaling, and more machines usually improve availability.

steps.prompt: After scaling out to 5 web servers, users get logged out at random. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Sessions are stored in each server's memory instead of a shared store
The servers have too little CPU

steps.explanation: If each server keeps sessions in its own memory, a request that lands on a different server can't find the session. Keeping servers stateless and storing sessions centrally (e.g. Redis) fixes it.
